description: Claudemaxxing is a Dnipro team taking on the Mars Map challenge: an interplanetary survival guide that turns NASA Mars data into a map a crew could use to pick a landing site, find water ice and stay alive. We build fast with AI tools and aim to demo a working prototype by the end of the weekend. Looking for: developers (Python), people into data analysis, visualization and stats, and anyone who knows ML or just loves Mars. We speak English, Ukrainian, Russian and German.
summary: AreoPath is a surface-walk (EVA) planner for the first astronauts on Mars. Existing tools such as JPL Mars Trek show Mars at regional and global scale, but a crew leaving a base needs a local answer: where can we walk, why there, and what don't we know? AreoPath layers data from several NASA missions around a base in Gale or Jezero crater, scores every ~460 m terrain cell for relative suitability, plans a least-cost route to a science target and marks what has not been assessed. Every value links to its source, and the 0–100 index is a transparent calculator for comparing sites, not a safety certificate. This answers the challenge's call for a layered, hyperlocal map that helps a human explorer plan a Marswalk safely while doing new science.
details:
What it does. AreoPath is designed as a tablet guide an astronaut carries on a surface walk. For two demo sites — Gale crater (Curiosity, Bradbury Landing) and Jezero crater (Perseverance) — a historical landing site acts as a hypothetical habitat. Around it the app shows:

- landing sites, water-ice evidence, mapped hazard zones (steep slopes, sand dunes) and science targets;

- a card for any point: relative suitability 0–100, advantages, risks, resources, hazard coverage (which hazards are assessed and which are not), elevation and data sources;

- historical environment context: surface radiation measured by Curiosity's RAD and archived weather from Perseverance MEDA and Curiosity REMS, clearly labelled as historical and not part of the score;

- a least-cost route from the base to a science target that avoids mapped hazards, limited to a 10 km demo EVA radius;

- a communications status bar with the Earth–Mars signal delay (~10.9 min one way on 15 Nov 2026) and relay passes via MRO/TGO.

How the score works. The area within 10 km of the base is split into ~460 m cells from MOLA topography. Each cell gets a 0–100 relative suitability index from four factors: slope (43 %), distance to the science target (29 %), surface roughness (14 %) and distance to base (14 %). Mapped hazards apply penalties. Cells beyond 10 km are excluded. Hazards we have no data for are shown as "not assessed", because unknown does not mean safe.

Why it matters. Mission planners and crews get one explainable view of a specific EVA instead of a global map. The same transparent calculator can be used in physics and astronomy classes, where students recompute scores and routes from real NASA data.

Technology. Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Leaflet, NASA JPL Mars Trek tiles. Backend: PHP API, Python scoring and data pipeline (ETL with tests), PostgreSQL, Docker, nginx with HTTPS on a VPS. Languages: TypeScript, Python, PHP. Hardware: none — runs in any modern browser on a laptop, tablet or phone.

Next steps. Walking vs crewed-rover travel modes, rover surface images along the route, radiation and space-weather layers, whole-crater terrain grids and USGS geologic maps.

Source code (MIT): https://github.com/misfonareher-web/claudemaxxing-mars-map

Use of AI. AI tools: Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 via Claude Code agents and chat; Google Gemini 4 Argon; OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex with GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6.1 Terra; Figma AI agent, used by Max for UI design. Under team direction, AI produced most code, ETL scripts, tests, audits, documentation and submission text drafts. Humans set scope and demo scenario, chose data and sources, reviewed outputs through spot checks and tests, handled deployment and gave final approval. Human review was selective, not line by line. Scores and routes are computed by deterministic code from NASA data, not generated by a language model. Some illustrative images in the demo slides are SI-generated and labelled as such; the product itself uses no AI image generation: the globe texture is scripted from MOLA data. The demo video is a real screen recording of the live app, with no AI-generated video or narration. The score is a heuristic, not a safety certification.
